details.text:
The Council's message ran four lines. A frontier colony called Hask Meadow had asked for "a Jedi" and would not say why. It was handed to the newest Knight on the roster, six days after your field restriction ended.

"Ten minutes, Knight," Pilot-Officer Ruddick says over the cockpit speaker. "Orders say I don't sit on an unsecured field after dark, and the sun is not cooperating with your schedule."

The ramp is down. The landing field is packed gravel and cracked ferrocrete, and a windsock hangs dead in the still air. The prefab hangar across the field has lost its door. It lies bent outward off its tracks, as though something inside left in a hurry, or something was let in that did not want to stay. Four parallel gouges score the wall beside it, about hip height on you. Paw prints in the dirt by the ramp are wider than your spread hand.

From the foot of the ramp the field opens flat in every direction. The hangar is about eighty feet to your left across open gravel. Sixty feet straight ahead, a split-rail fence marks the field's edge, with the gate in it. Beyond the gate, some ninety feet of long grass runs to the treeline, and a dirt lane leaves the gate and bends away along the trees toward the settlement.

At the field's edge, a hand-painted board hangs on a gate: PLEASE LEAVE THE GATE AS YOU FOUND IT. The gate is open.

A lanky teenager stands at the foot of the ramp with a lantern in one hand and a sheet of cardboard in the other. It reads JEDI??. The second question mark was added later, in a different pen.

"You're the Jedi," he says. "The Warden said they'd send someone. She didn't say they'd send someone who looks like... never mind. I'm Wick. I'm supposed to get you inside before the dogs wake up. It's four hundred meters. It's four hundred meters if we go *now*."

From the treeline beyond the gate, a woman's voice calls, warm and close to cracking:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The lantern stops moving. Wick does not turn toward the voice.

"Don't answer that," he says, very quietly. "Please."

Ruddick's ten minutes have started. What does Aero do?

details.text:
"What are the dogs," you ask, "and what happened to that hangar?"

Your thumb finds the activator. The indigo blade comes out of the hilt with a snap-hiss and settles into its hum, and the gravel at the foot of the ramp turns violet for ten feet in every direction. Wick's lantern jerks. He looks at the blade, then past it, at the field.

"They're ours," he says. "The drover-dogs. Nine of them. Biscuit runs them. The little kids named them all after snacks, which seemed funny before." He swallows. "They slept in the hangar at night. Then they got big. Bigger than dogs get. And they started looking at you like they were counting. One night they took the door off from the inside and didn't come back in."

You crouch at the edge of the blade's light and look at the ground.

The prints are not one animal's. Where the gravel thins into soft dirt beside the ramp you count five separate sets, the largest wider than your spread hand, claws pressed deep at the front of each pad. The ramp's foot sits on the edge of one of them: they were here before the shuttle touched down. They come from the direction of the hangar, eighty feet to your left. They do not run. They walk, spaced apart in a loose line, across the open gravel toward the gate sixty feet ahead of you, and through it, and into the long grass beyond, and there the dirt gives way to stems and you lose them.

Across the field, the claw marks on the hangar wall are not a single scrape. They are the same four strokes, again and again, at the height of your hip. Something stood up against that wall on its hind legs, more than once, and dragged its weight down it.

"Can we go now?" Wick says. "Please. I'll tell you the rest walking."

From the treeline, a hundred and fifty feet away past the open gate, the woman calls again.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same words. The same catch of breath before *honey*. The same crack at the end, in exactly the same place.

Wick's knuckles are white on the lantern handle. He does not turn around.

Behind you, the shuttle's engines tick as they cool. About nine of Ruddick's ten minutes are left.

details.text:
"All right," you say. "Stay at my shoulder, inside the light. We go now."

Wick doesn't need telling twice. He falls in at your right shoulder, close enough that the saber's violet wash catches the side of his face, and drops the lantern low so it lights the ground instead of him.

Before you step off the ramp's foot you reach for him through the Force, the way you were taught: not words, just weather.

It comes back strong. He is frightened all the way down, a high thin fear that has been running for days. Under it, every time the treeline speaks, something in him leans toward the sound and is hauled back by main strength, the way you'd hold yourself back from running to family. And under that, quieter and harder, there is something settled. Not a wish. A decision he has already made, folded small and kept out of sight, that he is not offering you.

His face shows none of it. He is looking at the gate.

You walk. Gravel crunches under two sets of boots. The blade's hum and the lantern's squeak are the loudest things on the field.

"Wick. Nine dogs, and I count five sets of tracks. Where are the other four?"

"I don't know." He doesn't slow down. "I don't know where Biscuit is either."

Sixty feet. The split-rail fence comes up out of the dusk and the open gate is right in front of you, the sign hanging crooked on it. PLEASE LEAVE THE GATE AS YOU FOUND IT. Beyond it the lane runs pale into the long grass and bends away along the trees, and the last of the daylight is going out of the sky over them.

From under those trees, about ninety feet past the gate, she calls again.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same breath before *honey*. The same crack at the end. Wick's step hitches and recovers.

And as you come into the gateway, the grass stops looking like grass.

Ahead and to the left of the lane, about twenty-five feet out and ten off the track, there is a long low shape lying in it, darker than the stems around it, a ridge of back that does not sway when the grass does. To the right, thirty feet out, another, flatter, the size of a man lying down. Further on the left, forty-five feet past the gate, a third, half-hidden, a pale smear of muzzle resting between forelegs.

None of them move. None of them has moved. They lie exactly along the lane you were about to walk down, on both sides of it, the way you would lay out a path.

They are well outside the blade's light. The lantern doesn't reach them either. You see them anyway.

Wick, at your shoulder, is still looking at the trees.

Behind you, back across sixty feet of open gravel, the shuttle sits with its ramp down and its running lights on. About eight and a half of Ruddick's minutes are left.

details.text:
"Wick," you say, low and even. "Don't look and don't run. There are dogs in the grass, both sides of the lane."

He does exactly what you tell him. His eyes stay on the trees. His whole body goes still, the way a rabbit's does, and the lantern stops swinging and hangs dead in his fist an inch above the dirt. You hear him breathe in through his nose and not let it out.

"Okay," he whispers.

The gate is right beside you, standing open on its post. You put your free hand to the top rail and swing it. It is heavier than it looks and the hinge complains, one long iron note that carries much too far across the grass. The latch drops into its keeper with a clack. The hand-painted board knocks once against the wood and settles. PLEASE LEAVE THE GATE AS YOU FOUND IT.

Now you stand just inside it, on the field side, Wick at your right shoulder. Between you and the long grass there are four horizontal rails of split timber with gaps between them a man could put his arm through. Twenty-five feet out to the left, thirty to the right, forty-five further out on the left, the three long shapes lie exactly where they lay. Flat. Heads down. Nothing moves in the grass.

And under the trees, ninety feet past the gate, the woman stops calling.

She does not finish a sentence and break off. There is simply no next time. You wait for the breath before *honey*, the crack at the end, and they do not come. The silence that replaces her is worse than the voice was. It has a shape.

You key your comlink.

It answers on the first chirp, Ruddick's voice thin and bright out of the little speaker at your collar, far too loud in all that quiet.

"Ruddick. Go ahead, Knight. I can see your blade at the fence. You've got about eight minutes."

The channel stays open. Behind you, sixty feet of grey gravel, the shuttle's running lights, the ramp still down. In front of you, the shut gate, the grass going from green to black, and three dogs that have not moved at all.

details.text:
"Wick." You keep your voice low and your eyes on the grass. "The voice stopped. Is there another way to the settlement that doesn't go through that grass?"

He doesn't look at you. He is still watching the trees, the way you told him to, and when he answers it comes out flat and quick, a runner giving directions.

"Yes. Along the fence to the corner, then the cart track up past the silos. It comes into the settlement from the top end." A breath. "It's twice as far. It's open the whole way, except where it crosses the ditch. The reeds are high there."

Your left hand finds the blaster at your hip and draws it. The grip is cold. Now the saber hums violet in your right hand and the pistol hangs ready in your left, and the closed gate is still between you and the long grass.

Thirty feet out, ahead and to the right of the lane, the second shape lies flat where it has lain since you first saw it. You reach for it through the Force, the way you reached for Wick: not words, just weather.

It is awake. It is not afraid of you. There is no guard dog's bristle in it, no cornered animal's heat. It is calm the way a hunter is calm, and it is patient.

Its attention is not all on you. Part of it rests on you and on the boy at your shoulder, steady as a hand on a rail, and part of it runs out sideways through the grass to the others lying there, and further, toward the trees, the way an ear turns toward a sound that has not come yet.

And under all of that there is something that is not dog.

It sits in the animal like a splinter of ice under a nail. Cold. Bright. Wrong. Something foreign set into it and left there, with an edge on it that every Jedi is taught to recognize: the dark side, small and sharp and humming.

You come back out of it. The grass is just grass again, going black.

You turn from the gate and start back toward the shuttle, and as you turn you look back over your shoulder, and the nearest dog, the one twenty-five feet out to the left, lifts its head.

It comes up out of the stems slowly, a broad wedge of skull on a thick neck, and it looks at you. Not at the gate. Not at Wick. At you. It holds there for the space of three of your steps, two dull points of the last grey sky caught in its eyes, and then it lowers its head and is a ridge of back in the grass again.

None of them rises. The trees stay silent.

The gravel crunches under your boots, and under Wick's, a little behind you now and falling further behind. You key the comlink at your collar without taking your eyes off the dark past the fence.

"Ruddick, I've got a way in that keeps out of the grass. I need more than seven minutes to walk it."

The channel hisses. For a long moment there is nothing on it but the shuttle's own noise coming up through the deck plates under your boots: the low tick of cooling metal, the idle whine of something in the drive housing that never quite stops. Behind you the cabin lights spill yellow across the top of the ramp. In front of you the gravel runs sixty feet to the shut gate, and past the gate the long grass is one flat black mass with no shapes in it at all.

You know where they were. Ninety-five feet, ahead and to the left. A hundred, ahead and to the right. A hundred and fifteen, further out on the left. And the fourth set of tracks, and the fifth, that you never saw lying down.

Then Ruddick's voice, thin out of the little speaker, closer to your ear than anything else in the field.

"Thirty minutes." A breath. "Not thirty-one. Your boots leave my ramp, it comes up and it stays up, and you call me the second you're inside the settlement. Thirty minutes from now, I lift."

The channel stays open. You can hear him breathing on the other end of it, waiting to see whether you argue.

Below you, ten feet down the pale slope of the ramp, Wick turns around.

For the first time since you told him not to, he takes his eyes off the trees. The lantern swings up with him and throws his shadow back across the gravel, long and thin toward the fence. His face is white in the light and set hard, and he looks straight up the ramp at you.

"I can take you," he says. Not loud. It still carries. "I know the track in the dark."

details.text:
You thumb the comlink at your collar. "Thank you, Ruddick. Thirty minutes. I'll call from inside."

"Copy." A click on the line. "Clock's running."

The channel stays open, a faint hiss against your ear, his breathing somewhere behind it.

You look down the ramp at the boy. "Then you lead, Wick, and you stay one step ahead of me where I can reach you. Nobody goes near that grass."

The words go out over the open channel too, and out across the field into the dark.

Wick nods once, hard, and turns. You go down the ramp after him. The moment your boots leave the metal, the hydraulics whine at your back; the ramp swings up behind you and seals with a deep thud you feel in your teeth, and the yellow wash of the hatch light is simply gone. The shuttle sits behind you as a dark hull and a few small running lights. What light there is now comes from two places: the violet hum of the blade in your right hand, and the lantern swinging low in Wick's fist a step ahead.

He takes you to the fence and turns east along the inside of it, the split rails at your left, waist-high, grey in the saber glow. Past the rails the long grass is a black wall. The gravel gives way to packed dirt and stubble. The blaster sits cold in your left hand.

As you walk you reach for him, the way you did at the gate. Not words. Weather.

He is frightened, wound tight as wire. But the offer was real: there is nothing crooked in it about the track, and something in him has loosened just from moving, from finally going somewhere. Under that, the pull is still there, toward the voice, the same as at the gate. And the settled thing you felt before, the intention, has a direction now. It does not lean toward the settlement. It leans out, past the rails, toward the trees and the voice. If it calls, he means to go to it.

And beneath the resolve, small and sour, something that feels like guilt. It is pointed at you.

You come back out of it. He is a step ahead, lantern low, exactly where you told him to be.

Twice on the walk he drifts. Half a step to the left, toward the rails, toward the grass, as if the ground were tilted that way. Both times he catches it and steps back into line without looking round.

About halfway along you hear it.

On the far side of the rails, out in the grass: a long, dry hush of stems parting, and parting again. Something heavy moving low, not hurrying. When you walk, it walks. When Wick's boot scuffs a stone and he checks for half a breath, the hush in the grass checks too. You cannot see anything out there. The saber light stops at the rails. Beyond them is only black, and the sound of the grass being pushed aside by something that is keeping pace with you.

You reach the corner. The fence turns south here to close the field's east side, and at the angle there is a gap in the rails where the cart track leaves the field: two pale ruts running out north into the dark. The shuttle is three hundred feet behind you now, a dim shape with its lights pricking the night.

The sound in the grass stops when you stop.

Then the voice.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same words. The same catch of breath before the last of them. But it is not behind you any more, under the trees by the lane where it has always been. It is ahead. Out past the corner, along the treeline, somewhere up the way the cart track runs.

Wick goes rigid a step in front of you. The lantern swings toward the sound and hangs there, the flame shivering behind its glass. He does not move his feet. You can hear him breathing, fast and shallow, through his teeth.

On your collar the comm hisses, open.

The echo of your own voice is still hanging under the trees when you speak again, low, to the back of Wick's head.

"Wick, if that thing can wear my voice, it can wear hers. I'm not saying she's gone. I'm saying that isn't her."

The channel at your collar is open. The words go out over it as well, a thin doubled echo in the hiss, and out across the dark in still air. Ruddick doesn't answer.

You thumb the activator. The indigo blade folds back into the hilt with a short falling hum, and the night closes in from every side at once. The hilt stays in your right hand, cold and dead, your thumb resting on the switch. The blaster is still in your left.

Wick doesn't answer for a long moment. You hear him breathing, fast and shallow through his nose. Then he looks down at the lantern in his fist, and with a small scrape of metal he slides its shutter almost closed. The light shrinks to a dim slit, a few feet of weak yellow at the height of his knee. Past that, nothing. The ruts, the grass, the trees are gone.

You lay your left hand on his shoulder, the blaster still in it, muzzle down, the back of your wrist against his collar. Not a grip. Enough to steer. He doesn't pull away. You turn him off the track, to the right, away from where the long grass stands, and he comes: three, four, five strides across the ruts and onto the pasture. The ground changes underfoot. Hard dirt gives way to short cropped stubble that crunches faintly no matter how you place your feet.

Then north. Slowly. Heel, then the rest of the foot. Wick matches you, his shoulder rising and falling under your wrist. The track is somewhere off to your left now, fifteen feet away and invisible; beyond it, the grass. Ahead, the trees, perhaps sixty feet off, darker than the dark around them. The slit of lantern light swings at his knee, and you can see your own boots in it and nothing else.

You listen as you go.

Nothing. No hush of stems parting to your left. Nothing behind you. No breathing. The grass that walked when you walked is not walking now, or not so you can hear it. The voice under the trees says nothing. On your collar, the comm hisses, open, and Ruddick stays silent on the other end of it.

Thirty feet across the stubble, the boy is still under your hand. The trees are closer. Whatever was in the grass, you cannot tell where it is now, or whether it lost you.

Ruddick's clock has about twenty-four minutes left on it.

You stop. Wick stops with you, his shoulder under the back of your wrist, the slit of lantern light hanging still at his knee. The stubble stops crunching. The quiet that comes in behind it is enormous.

Fifteen feet to your left, the cart track, invisible. Beyond it, the long grass. Somewhere behind you, ninety feet back, the gap in the fence. Ahead, sixty feet off, the trees: a band of black against black, felt more than seen.

You keep your voice low.

"Wick, where does the track go once it reaches the trees? How far to the first buildings?"

The comm at your collar is open. The question goes out over it as well, a thin echo in the hiss, and out into the still air in every direction at once.

Wick doesn't turn his head. When he answers, it is barely a breath.

"It goes straight through. It's only a strip there, the trees. Forty strides, maybe." A swallow. "Then it's open grazing down to the ditch. Then up the rise to the silos. The silos are the first thing. The barns are by them." A pause. "Half a klick. Bit more."

Then, quieter still:

"She called from there. Right where the track goes in."

His shoulder doesn't move under your hand. It has gone hard as wood, and the whole of him is turned toward that one patch of dark, ahead and a little to the left, where the ruts run into the trees.

You listen.

Nothing. No hush of stems parting in the grass across the track. Nothing behind you. No breathing. The trees give back no voice: not his mother's, not yours. On your collar the channel hisses, open, and Ruddick says nothing.

It is the silence of a room where someone is holding their breath.

A minute gone, standing here. Ruddick's clock has about twenty-three minutes left on it, and the silos are a little over half a klick away, through the strip of trees where the voice called.

The back of your wrist is still against Wick's shoulder. You keep your voice under the hiss of the channel.

"Then we go through together, quietly, and we don't stop for anything we hear in there."

It goes out over the comm as well, a thin twin of your own voice at your collar, and out into the still air in every direction at once. Ruddick doesn't answer.

You listen to the trees.

Sixty feet ahead, the band of black where the ruts run in. You give it everything you have: breath held, mouth open, head a little turned. Nothing comes back. No breathing, no shift of weight, no voice. Your own pulse, loud in your ears. The channel, hissing. Whatever is under those trees, if anything is, the dark keeps it.

Wick doesn't turn his head. His whisper is barely there.

"And if it's her?"

He doesn't wait for an answer.

You move.

The stubble crunches under your boots, then under his. A few strides, a walking pace, and your hand comes away from his shoulder; the boy keeps step beside you, close enough to touch, the slit of lantern light swinging at his knee. The dark hilt sits in your right hand, thumb on the activator. The blaster hangs muzzle-down in your left. Fifteen feet to your left, the cart track, two pale ruts you can barely make out. Beyond it, the long grass.

Halfway to the trees, the grass beyond the track starts to move with you.

Not loud. A long hush of stems pressed aside, low to the ground, on your left. Heavy. More than one. When you lengthen your stride it lengthens. Then it is not grass any more but leaf litter, a dry pad and shift among the trunks on the far side of the track: the same weight, the same pace, keeping level with you in the dark. You cannot see any of it. You cannot tell how many.

The trees take you in.

It is colder under them, and darker than dark: the sky goes, the stars go, and what is left is the smell of bark and wet earth and the small sick glow at Wick's knee lighting nothing but his boots and a few feet of root and needle. Trunks loom up out of nothing and slide past. Sixty feet in, the middle of the strip, the far edge somewhere ahead, another sixty feet, invisible.

Then, from among the trees on your left, just across the track, twenty-five feet away. Close enough to throw a stone.

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same words. The same small catch of breath. Exactly as before, at the gate, from the treeline. Exactly.

Wick goes rigid beside you, within reach of your hand. The lantern slit swings toward the voice and stops there, shaking, lighting nothing. He does not answer it. He does not take a step. You can hear him breathing, quick and shallow through his nose, and nothing else: the voice has stopped, and the weight that was keeping pace on the left has stopped with it.

The channel hisses at your collar. About twenty-two minutes left on Ruddick's clock. Sixty feet of trees ahead of you, sixty feet behind, and the voice, twenty-five feet to your left, waiting for an answer.

details.text:
The voice has stopped. Wick's breathing hasn't. You lean in until your mouth is near his ear and keep it low, under the hiss at your collar.

"Don't answer it, Wick. Stay with me. Eyes ahead."

The words go out over the open channel too, a thin second copy of you at your throat, and into the still air between the trunks. Ruddick doesn't answer.

Your thumb moves.

The blade comes out of the hilt with a snap-hiss that is far too loud under the trees, and then the hum settles, low and steady, and the dark around you is indigo. Ten feet of it. Bark, wet and furrowed. Roots like knuckles. Needles. Wick's face, white, sweat on his lip. Past ten feet the light simply stops, and the trees beyond it are blacker than before.

Your left hand still holds the blaster. Your right holds the blade. You tell Wick to open the lantern.

His fingers shake on the slide. It grates, sticks, then goes all the way, and yellow light spills out around his boots and up his legs, a little short of the blade's reach. He lifts it, not much.

"She'll see the light," he whispers.

Then he turns his face forward. Eyes ahead.

You stand still and listen to the left.

Across the track, among the trees, where the weight was keeping pace. You give it the same as before: breath held, head turned, the hum of the blade in your hand and the hiss at your collar. Nothing comes back. No breathing. No pad on the leaf litter. Whatever walked beside you through the grass has gone still, or gone. The dark beyond the light gives you nothing at all.

You walk.

Sixty feet of trees. The two lights move together, indigo and yellow, and the trunks swim up out of the black and slide past and go back into it. Nothing crosses the light. Nothing moves on the left that you can hear. Then the canopy thins, and there is sky again, stars, and the open grazing pale under them, and you step out onto it.

Behind you, from inside the trees, your own voice says:

"Don't answer it, Wick. Stay with me. Eyes ahead."

Your voice. Your pitch, your breath, the little drop you put on "ahead". From the dark you have just walked out of.

Wick's whole body jerks. The lantern swings. He doesn't stop. He doesn't look back. His boots keep going, and so do yours.

Nothing else comes.

The grazing is cropped short and grey, a thousand feet of it, and the light you carry makes a small moving room in the middle of it. The track runs ahead as two pale ruts. The trees fall behind, a black wall, then a black line. Nothing follows that you can see. Nothing follows that you can hear: only your boots, his boots, the hum, the hiss, his breathing.

The ground dips. Reeds stand higher than Wick's head along the drainage ditch, rattling dry against the blade's light where the track fords it. The water is a few inches deep and cold through your boots. Then you're up the far bank and climbing, seven hundred feet of gentle rise, and the shapes at the top grow out of the dark until they're buildings.

Three silos in a row, tall and blind. Two barns beside them, doors shut. No light in any of them. The middle silo's door has a bar across it, and in your light the seam is lumpy with fresh weld beads, bright metal on old.

Wick lifts the lantern and points down a lane past the barns. About three hundred feet on, a long, low hall, and light leaking thin and gold at the seams of its shutters.

"The Grange," he says.

No one is outside. The channel hisses at your collar. About fifteen minutes left on Ruddick's clock, and Ruddick is waiting for a call.

details.text:
The silos stand over you, three black drums against a sky with almost nothing left in it. The middle one's door is a slab of shadow at the edge of your light, the bar across it, the weld beads along the seam catching indigo like a row of blisters.

You thumb the comm at your collar. The channel is already open; it has been open the whole way.

"Ruddick, we're at the silos. Grange is in sight. Keep the ramp sealed."

A breath of hiss. Then his voice, small and flat at your throat.

"Copy, Knight. You're in. Ramp's sealed and it stays sealed. Clock doesn't change: fifteen minutes, then I lift."

The channel goes back to hissing. He doesn't sign off.

You slide the blaster into its holster. Your left hand is empty now; your right still holds the blade, low, humming, ten feet of indigo light around you and the boy.

Wick doesn't say anything. He lifts the lantern and falls in beside you.

The lane runs down from the silos between the two barns, packed earth with a grass strip up the middle where the cart wheels never touched. The barns go by on either side, close enough to touch: plank walls, a big door on rollers, shut, a smaller one, shut. Your light slides over them and lets them go. Hay smell. Old engine oil. Animal smell, faint and stale, the kind that stays in wood after the animals have gone. No sound comes out of either barn. Nothing moves in the black gaps between them, or on the lane ahead, or behind.

Halfway down, Wick turns his head and looks back up the rise. The silos. The dark beyond them, where the ditch is, and the grazing, and the line of trees you can no longer see. He looks for a second, two. Then he faces front again and keeps step, close enough to touch.

Your boots. His boots. The hum of the blade. The hiss at your collar.

The Grange comes up out of the dark as a wall: long, low, timbered, the roof running away into black on both sides. The shutters are closed. Thin lines of yellow light show at their seams, the same lines you saw from the silos, steady, unchanged. The door is wide, heavy, plank on plank, iron at the hinges. Shut.

No one opens it. No shadow crosses the light at the seams. No voice comes from inside.

You stand at the door with Wick at your shoulder, the lantern in his hand and the blade in yours, a pool of light on the step and the dark all around it. Somewhere back across the field, on Ruddick's clock, thirteen minutes are left.

details.text:
The door is close enough to touch: planks laid on planks, the grain gone grey, iron straps at the hinges the width of your hand. Light leaks at the shutter seams to either side of it, thin and yellow and steady. Behind you, ten feet of indigo on the step, and then the dark.

Before you raise your hand you ask Wick to keep watch behind you. The words go out at your collar too, into the open channel, into the hiss.

Wick doesn't answer. He turns his back to the door, to you, and lifts the lantern toward the lane. His shoulder is against your arm. The light he holds runs up the packed earth a little way and stops: the grass strip down the middle, the corner of the near barn, a roller door, shut. Past that, nothing. He stands there with the lantern up and his breath going short and quiet, watching the way you came.

Nothing moves in it.

You knock with your left hand. The blade hums low in your right.

"Hask Meadow. I'm the Jedi you asked for. Open the door."

The knock goes into the wood and the wood gives back almost nothing. On the channel, Ruddick says nothing.

Then, from inside, close, right behind the planks: a bolt drawn back. Iron on iron, slow, as if whoever is doing it does not want to be heard doing it.

The door moves. A hand's width, no more, and a chain snaps taut across the gap at the height of your chest.

Warm air comes out through it, and smell: smoke, bodies, too many people in a closed room for too long, boiled grain, wet wool. Behind that, a murmur that stops all at once, the way a room stops when everyone in it turns to look.

In the gap, a face. A man, unshaven, the skin under his eyes dark as bruises, lit yellow from behind and indigo from in front. Below the face, low, the long muzzle of a hunting rifle, held at the level of your belt. It does not point at you. It does not point away.

His eyes go to the blade first. Then past it, past you, to the boy with his back turned and the lantern raised.

"Wick?"

Wick doesn't turn. The lantern stays up, pointed at the lane.

The man doesn't take his eyes off the two of you. He speaks over his shoulder, into the hall, not loud.

"It's Hallan's boy. And one with a light."

Nobody in the hall answers him. The chain stays on. The rifle stays where it is.

Up the lane, the dark. At your collar, the hiss. On Ruddick's clock, about twelve minutes.

details.text:
The chain hangs taut at the height of your chest. Through the gap, the man's face and the rifle held low; behind him, the long hall's yellow light and the murmur of a great many people being quiet. At your arm, Wick, his back to the door, the lantern up, the lane beyond it empty as far as the light goes and black after that.

"My pilot lifts in about eleven minutes, with or without me. Tell the Warden that."

The man's eyes stay on you. At your collar, the words go out into the open channel, into the hiss.

You keep talking, to the hiss this time.

"Ruddick, can you search for a spot to land over here or hover at least? I can grapple up with some synthrope if I must. But if you leave, so help me, at first light I will have you on trial."

A pause on the channel. Long enough to hear the shuttle's cabin behind it, the low tick of something cooling, the faint whine of systems held warm.

Then Ruddick, flat and close at your collar, loud in the stillness of the step:

"You want it on the record? Put this on it." A breath. "Five minutes. Then I lift."

The channel stays open. He says nothing else.

Beside you, Wick doesn't turn. The lantern doesn't move. His voice comes low, toward the lane, not toward you.

"You're going back to the ship."

Through the gap, the man has heard every word from your collar. He looks at it, then past you at the boy. Then he steps back and to the side, and the yellow strip of light across your boots widens, narrows, and someone else is in the gap.

A woman, about sixty. Grey hair pulled back hard. She stands straight, the way people stand who have counted things for a living, and she doesn't touch the chain. Her eyes go over you once: your face, the dead hilt in your right hand, the comlink at your collar. Then to Wick's back, and they stay there a moment longer than they stayed on you.

"You're late, Jedi."

The chain stays where it is. She doesn't say anything else. She waits.

Up the lane, the dark. Somewhere far behind it, past the silos, past the strip of trees, across the field, a shuttle with its ramp sealed and about five minutes on its clock. At your collar, the hiss.

details.text:
Ten feet of gravel between you and the step. The blade's light reaches the door and stops there: the grain of the planks, the iron links of the chain, and in the gap behind it, her face, half indigo, half the hall's yellow. The man with the rifle is a shape behind her shoulder. At your side, within reach, Wick, facing up the lane into nothing.

"Nobody came then. I came now. Decide what that's worth before my ride does."

The words go out at your collar too, into the hiss.

Your left hand goes to your hip and comes up with the blaster. The blade stays where it is in your right, humming, the light steady on the step.

You tell Wick to open the lantern. He doesn't answer. The shutter scrapes back, and yellow light spills out over the indigo and runs a little further up the lane than the blade can: the gravel, the ruts, the dark sides of the two shut barns.

"Ruddick - leave and don't come back. You're fired. You are not being paid for this misssion and I'll see to it that you are fined and stripped of your license."

You close the channel before anything comes back. The hiss at your collar stops. For the first time since the field, there is nothing there at all: no cabin tick, no breathing, no voice. Just the blade's hum, and the lantern's small hot creak, and the boy beside you.

Behind the chain, her eyes have gone to your collar. They stay there a moment after the hiss is gone.

"Warden, I cannot lower my blade until I know that Wick and I are safe. You're making decisions but I can't help you if you don't let me in. I'll find shelter up the lane to the silos - I am trying to help, but you must let me. When you're ready, come find me. Unless you're okay with your loved one dying because of your obstinance."

No channel carries it this time. It goes only as far as the step, the gap, the woman, the man behind her, and Wick.

You give her the moment.

She doesn't look at you. She looks past your arm, at the boy and his open lantern.

"Wick."

Once. Then the door closes. The gap goes to a line and the line goes out, and the yellow strip on the gravel is gone. On the other side, the chain rattles off its run and something heavy goes across the inside of the door with a wooden thud. The step is just a step now, planks and a shut door in the blade's light.

You turn on your heel and go.

The lane climbs between the two barns, gravel crunching under your boots, the blade's hum going with you and the dark closing again behind it. Ten paces. Twenty. You don't wait. Behind you, nothing for a moment. Then quick footsteps on the gravel, and the lantern light swings up beside you, jittering, and steadies.

Wick is at your shoulder again, within reach, breathing hard through his nose.

"You said you'd be right here."

He says it low, not looking at you. He doesn't stop walking.

Then the night behind the silos opens up.

It starts as a pressure you feel in your teeth before you hear it: repulsors, far off past the top of the rise, past the grazing and the strip of trees. Then the engines catch, and the sound rolls over the meadow in one long tearing wave, loud even here, loud enough that the boy's head jerks up. Above the black line of the far trees a cluster of running lights lifts, hangs a moment, tilts, and climbs. It gets smaller. The roar thins to a whine, then a hum, then nothing. The lights become one light, then a point, then a space among the stars where a point was.

The meadow is very quiet after that.

You keep walking. The lane flattens out, and the silos are there, three of them in a row at the top of the rise, tall and dark, two barns shut beside them. Your light finds the middle one's door: the bar across it, the seam lumpy with weld beads, bright metal on old. Nothing moves on it. Nothing moves anywhere your light goes.

Down the lane behind you, about three hundred feet, the Grange is a long dark shape with thin yellow lines at its shutters. The door is shut. Beyond the silos, the rise falls away to the grazing, the ditch, the strip of trees where your own voice called back to you, and past that a field with nothing on it.

Wick stands beside you with the lantern held out toward the dark. The blade hums in your right hand. The blaster is cold in your left. Your collar is silent.

details.text:
The silos stand over you, three tall dark curves at the top of the rise. Wick is at your right shoulder, within reach, the open lantern in his fist. The blade hums in your right hand; the blaster sits in your left. Your collar is silent. The channel is closed, and nothing you say tonight goes anywhere but into the air.

"I did say that. I'm still here, Wick. So are you."

He doesn't answer. His breath goes in and out through his nose, fast, then slower.

You give it a moment. Then: "She called you in by name. Who is she to you? Who's she waiting for out there? And what the hell was going on in the woods?"

"She's the Warden." He keeps his eyes on the dark past the light. "Marga Tolliver. She runs Hask. She's the one said I couldn't go out."

A breath.

"Garrick. Her son. He's one of the six." His jaw works. "With my mam."

The lantern trembles, a little, and steadies.

"The dogs. Ours. They walked with us the whole way through the trees." He swallows. "And it was her voice. Same words, every time. Like you said." He looks at you, once, quickly. "Like yours."

Your voice comes out harder. "No ship, no door. Then we do this ourselves. Tell me everything you know about that silo. And keep the light up and stay at my shoulder. Nothing gets between us."

The lantern comes up. He stays where he is, at your shoulder, close enough that his sleeve brushes your arm.

"Silo Three." He nods at the middle one without taking his eyes off it. "The seed silo. The Warden had her people weld it and bar it. The day after the dogs went wrong. Nobody goes up there." A pause. "Garrick's crew was digging under it all season. Making the seed vault bigger." Quieter. "Then they stopped."

You look.

The light doesn't go far: ten feet, twenty, indigo and yellow laid over gravel, and then the dark takes it. Inside it, the curved bases of the three silos, rust-streaked, cold. Against the left-hand one, a handcart, and on it a welding torch and two gas bottles, left where somebody set them down and walked away. Under the middle silo's seam, on the gravel, a grey spatter of slag, the drips frozen where they fell. The bar across the door. The welds, lumpy and bright on old metal.

At the edge of the light, the two barns, doors shut. Past the light there is nothing. Not the grazing, not the ditch, not the trees. Black, and down the lane the Grange's thin yellow lines, and that is all. Nothing moves anywhere your eyes can reach.

Then, from far down the rise, from the dark where the strip of trees must be, faint enough that at first it could be the wind, except there is no wind:

"Wick? Wick, honey, where are you? I can't find the path."

The same words. The same catch of breath before *honey*. Thin with distance, a third of a mile of night between you and it, and still exactly the same.

Wick goes still beside you. The lantern doesn't move. Neither does he.

Nothing else comes. No second call. No sound in the grass. The meadow lies there, quiet.

You walk to the nearer barn, thirty feet, the gravel loud under your boots. Wick comes with you, at your shoulder, the lantern up, his free hand closed tight around nothing. The light climbs the barn's plank front as you close on it: grey boards, a latch, and across the gap between the doors a hasp, a heavy chain through it, and a padlock hanging off the chain.

You pull. The doors shift a finger's width against the chain and stop. The chain clinks. The lock holds.

Behind you the silos stand in the dark, thirty feet back. Down the lane, about two hundred eighty feet off, the Grange is unchanged: the door shut, the yellow lines at the shutters steady. Out past the rise, the trees say nothing more.

Wick is beside you, breathing, the lantern held high, looking back the way the voice came.

The chain hangs across the shed door where it has hung all along, the padlock a cold fist against the hasp. Wick is at your right shoulder, within reach, the lantern up. Thirty feet behind you, Silo Three stands barred in the dark. Down the lane, about two hundred eighty feet off, the Grange keeps its thin yellow lines. Your collar is silent; the channel is closed.

"Thank you, Wick. You've told me more tonight than anyone in that hall."

He doesn't answer that. He nods, once, short, his eyes still on the dark.

"When did the digging stop? Before the dogs went wrong, or after?"

"Before." It comes quickly, then he slows down. "A few days before. Garrick's crew came down off the rise and that was it. They were done." He shifts the lantern to his other fist. "Early. Nobody thought anything of it."

"She chained a tool shed and welded a silo, and left six people outside. I want to know why."

Wick looks at the padlock, then down the lane at the shut hall.

"Me too."

That is all he says. The lantern comes back up.

You slide the blaster into its holster on your right hip. The grip settles against your side. Your left hand is empty now; the blade still hums in your right, indigo on the gravel.

You look across at the cart.

It sits against the curve of the left-hand silo, about thirty-five feet away, where your light thins out and gives up. A two-wheeled handcart. A gas-welding torch lies on it at the end of a coiled hose, and behind the torch two tall gas bottles stand strapped upright, each one about as high as your waist. The hose still runs from the torch back to the regulators on the bottles; nobody uncoupled it. The torch tip is black with old burn.

In the gravel, two narrow ruts run from the cart's wheels toward Silo Three's door, through the grey spatter of slag, and back again. Somebody pushed it up to that door, and worked there, and pushed it back.

From here, that is what the light gives you. The cart is still thirty-five feet off, and the bottles are not things that go into a backpack.

Down the rise, the dark goes on to where the strip of trees must be.

Nothing calls. Nothing moves in the grass. Wick breathes beside you, the lantern high, and the blade hums.

details.text:
The shed door is in front of you, unlatched, the cut chain in a heap at its foot with the padlock still locked on it. Wick is at your right shoulder, within reach, the lantern lowered onto the boards. Thirty feet behind you Silo Three stands barred in the dark; the welding cart sits about thirty-five feet off against the left-hand silo, at the edge of the light. Down the lane, about two hundred eighty feet away, the Grange keeps its thin yellow lines. Your collar is silent.

"Open it on my word. Slow."

Wick sets his free hand on the handle and waits. Then, on your word, he pulls.

The door comes toward you an inch at a time, swinging out over the gravel. Its bottom edge drags with a low scrape of wood on stone, and that is all. No shriek of hinges. The sound is gone in the cold air almost as soon as it starts.

Cold comes out of the shed to meet you, colder than the night, and with it a smell: machine oil, damp soil, old fuel.

Wick's lantern goes in first.

A repulsor hauler sled sits nose to the door, powered down, its bed caked with dried earth. Along the left wall, tools hang in their racks where someone put them back: spades, picks, a soil auger, coils of cable, a stack of shoring planks. Fuel drums stand against the right wall. Just inside the door to the right there is a workbench, and on it a crew work datapad, dark. Above the bench a sheet of flimsi is pinned to the boards: a site chart, drawn by hand, of the ground under Silo Three. A shaft is marked under the silo's base, with depths written beside it in a cramped column.

Past the hauler, past about twenty feet, the light gives out. The back of the shed is black.

You look. Into the shed, and then around you, as far as the light will carry.

The floor in there is packed earth under a skin of dust. Old boot prints run through it, back and forth between the door and the hauler, their edges soft. None of them are fresh. There are no paw prints at all. On the door frame, just inside, there is a switch box with a heavy lever, and a cable runs from it up the wall to a glowpanel strip under the roof beam. The lever is down. Whether there is any power behind it, there is no way to tell from here.

Outside, the light shows you gravel, the curved bases of the silos, the cart at the edge of the glow. Nothing moves. Not in the shed, not on the rise, not in the lane.

You draw the blaster from your right hip into your left hand. The grip is cold. The blade still hums in your right, indigo on the gravel.

Then you turn, and put your back to Wick's.

He faces into the shed with the lantern. You face out, over the lane and the dark, toward the rise and the trees you cannot see from here. His shoulder blades are against yours. Through your robes you can feel him breathing, quick and shallow.

He says nothing. Behind you his light moves slowly over the hauler and the walls, and comes back to the door.

Nothing calls from the trees. Nothing moves in the grass. The blade hums.

details.text:
You stand in the open doorway of the dig crew's shed with your back against Wick's. He faces in with the lantern; you face out, over the gravel and the curved bases of the silos, toward the lane and the long black slope of the rise. The blade is lit in your right hand, the blaster in your left. Far down the rise, about a third of a mile off, the strip of trees is a darker line against the dark. Nothing calls from it.

"You're doing fine, Wick. Keep your back to mine. I've got the dark."

Through your robes you feel him draw a breath.

"Yeah," he says, quietly. The lantern stays up.

You turn from the lane. You step past him through the doorway, and the cold of the shed closes over you, oil and damp soil and old fuel. Five feet in, the workbench is at your right hip, the dark datapad on it, the flimsi chart pinned above. Wick comes in behind you and stops just inside the door, within a step of you.

He reaches back, takes the inner edge of the door and pulls it to. It comes in over the gravel with the same low scrape as before, wood on stone, and meets the frame. The lane is gone. The silos are gone. The night is a few thin seams of black between the boards.

In the light, on the inside of the door, there are two iron brackets bolted to either side of the frame, made to take a drop bar. A length of shoring plank leans against the wall beside them. It would fit. It is not in place.

"Breathe slow. Nothing's moving out here. Nothing's in there with us."

You slide the blaster into its holster on your right hip. Your left hand is empty.

The switch box is on the frame beside Wick's shoulder, within reach. You take the heavy lever and throw it.

It goes up with a clack that is loud in the closed shed, metal on metal.

Nothing else happens. The glowpanel strip under the roof beam stays dark. No flicker, no hum. There is no power behind it. The lever stays where you put it, and your hand comes away.

So the light is what you brought: the indigo of the blade, the yellow of Wick's lantern, and past twenty feet, nothing.

You take the work datapad off the bench in your left hand. It is cold and a little gritty with dust, its screen black. You do not switch it on.

You look up at the chart. The flimsi has curled at the corners around its pins. In the mixed light the shaft is drawn going straight down from the base of Silo Three, a single ruled line, and beside it runs the cramped column of depths, in metres, in a small hard hand. The deepest number is 13.5. You give it a minute. Whatever else is on the sheet, the light and the scrawl do not give it up to you.

Then you look into the dark past the hauler, as far as the light will go. The hauler's far flank, the dried earth crusted on its bed. Behind it the floor's dust lies smooth and grey right to the edge of the light. Not a print in it. Not a boot, not a paw. No one has walked back there since that dust settled.

You ask Wick to guard the door.

He turns to face it, the open lantern in his hand, his back to you now.

You go back past the hauler with the blade held out ahead of you. Its glow pushes into the dark ten feet at a time and the dark gives way just that much. Your boots leave the only marks in the dust.

At the back of the shed, about thirty feet from the door: four crew lockers standing against the wall, all shut. A folding cot with a blanket thrown over it. A space heater, cold. A stack of curved lining panels, the kind meant to wall a vault, waiting for a hole to go into. Behind all of it the back wall is plain boards, end to end. There is no other door. The only way in or out is the one Wick is holding.

You speak back down the length of the shed to him.

"That chart over the bench. Did you ever see Garrick's crew go down that shaft?"

The lantern does not move from the door. "No. They never let anybody up here while they worked." A pause. "You'd just hear the hauler going up and down the lane. And the winch, at night sometimes."

"You think that hauler still runs? What time does it get light around here and what time is it currently?"

"It ran. Every day, till they stopped." He glances back at it, at the dirt on its bed, then at the door again. "Don't know now." His breath smokes in the lantern light. "Sun went down maybe three-quarters of an hour ago. And light..." He lets out a short breath that is almost a laugh and is not. "Not for ages. Thirteen hours, about, this time of year."

The shed creaks once, the way old boards do in the cold. The blade hums in your hand. Outside, through the seams in the door, nothing moves that you can see, and nothing calls.

details.text:
The back of the shed is cold enough that your breath shows in the blade's light. Thirty feet away, at the shut door, Wick is a small shape behind the yellow of the lantern, his back to you, facing the boards.

"Thirteen hours is a long time, Wick. We'll spend it smart. Stay with the light."

The lantern doesn't move. "Okay," he says.

You reach your left hand over your shoulder and push the work datapad down into your pack, its screen still black, its edges still gritty. The pack settles. Your left hand is empty again; the blade hums on in your right.

Then you look, close.

The four lockers stand shoulder to shoulder against the back wall, plain grey metal, dented at the corners. Each has a lever latch. None has a lock on it. Someone has stencilled names on strips across the tops of the doors: HADDOW. PELL. VARRO. G. TOLLIVER. You run the light along all four. The doors stay shut. You leave them shut.

The cot beside them has a blanket thrown over it, creased long-ways where someone lay on it. The space heater is cold to the hand, its cord running down the wall to a socket, still plugged in. The lining panels are stacked in their curved sheets, new, coated in a skin of dust. Nobody has touched them since they were unloaded.

That is all three minutes of looking gives you.

You walk back up the shed, fifteen feet, past the end of the hauler sled, until its dirt-caked nose is beside your knee. Wick and the door are fifteen feet ahead now, the switch box on the frame at his shoulder, lit yellow by the lantern.

You follow the cable with your eyes. It leaves the top of the box and climbs the door frame, runs along the roof beam above you to the dead glowpanel strip. One drop comes down a post to a charging socket by the hauler's nose. Another runs along the wall, back into the dark, to the heater's socket. The feed comes into the bottom of the box out of the wall, low beside the door frame, where the boards meet the gravel.

From here, nothing looks wrong. The lever is up. There is no light.

"The winch you heard at night. Was that before the dogs went wrong, or after?"

Wick doesn't answer at once. The lantern's flame leans and straightens.

"After," he says. "After the dogs went wrong. One night, late." He swallows; you hear it in the quiet. "Then the Warden's people welded the silo."

Outside, beyond the boards, nothing calls. The seams between them are black. The shed is silent again.

details.text:
The hauler's nose is cold beside your knee. Fifteen feet ahead, Wick stands at the shut door with the lantern, its yellow on the boards and on the plank leaning beside the brackets.

"Drop that plank in the brackets, Wick. Nothing comes through that door tonight."

He looks down at the plank. The lantern stays up. "Okay," he says. He doesn't reach for it. One hand holds the light; the plank is a two-handed weight.

"One night, after. Did you see anyone go up to the silo? A light, the hauler, anything?"

"No." He shakes his head without turning round. "I didn't go look. I just heard it, a long way off, and then it stopped."

You turn to the sled.

It is a flatbed about ten feet long, nose to the door. At the nose stands a waist-high driver's stand with a tiller bar across it. A key sits in the key switch, turned to off. The charge gauge beside it is dark glass. Tie-down rings run along both rails of the bed, and the bed itself is caked with dug earth gone hard, studded with broken grey stone. Its charging lead hangs coiled on the post by the nose, not plugged into anything.

You give it two minutes under the blade. It gives you nothing more. Whether it would run, you still don't know.

You walk the fifteen feet up to the door. Wick shifts to make room, and you stand at his shoulder under the switch box.

Close up, by the blade and the lantern together, the box is plain. Lever up. Cover latched. No scorch on the metal, no smell of burning. Then you look lower.

Under the box, where the feed comes in out of the wall, a heavy plug hangs on its cable, a hand's width below its socket. Not broken. Not burnt. Out.

That is why there is no light.

You thumb the blade off. The indigo goes out of the shed all at once, and the dark comes in from the back wall to the edge of the lantern's reach: the door, the frame, the box, Wick's face, ten feet of packed earth floor. The hauler is a shape. The lockers at the back are gone into the dark.

You clip the hilt to your left hip. Both your hands are empty.

Wick sets the lantern down on the workbench by the door. Between you, you take the plank. It is heavier than it looks, rough under your palms. You lift it together and drop it into the brackets across the door.

It seats with one wooden thud.

Nobody is pulling that door open from outside now.

You look at the switch box again, by lantern light alone. The lever is up. The plug hangs where it hung. Nothing has changed.

Outside, beyond the boards, nothing calls. The gaps between them are black. Wick's breath and yours are the only sounds in the shed.
